analysis.one_liner: Restricts payday-style lenders, blocks fees, and stops selling bank account access.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on September 19, 2024, and died there when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The SAFE Lending Act would tighten rules on small-dollar lenders, the industry behind online payday and installment loans up to $5,000. It would require those lenders to register with the consumer protection bureau, apply the interest-rate and fee caps of the state where the borrower lives, and stop middlemen from selling borrowers' bank account numbers and Social Security numbers to lenders. It would also let borrowers block lenders from reaching into their bank accounts with unsigned electronic checks, ban overdraft fees on prepaid accounts, and order a study of small-dollar lending on Indian reservations. The bill was introduced in September 2024 with four Democratic cosponsors, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who use online payday, installment, and similar small-dollar loans. These are typically lower-income households facing a cash crunch. The bill would give them three things: their state's rate and fee caps would follow them online no matter where the lender is chartered; they could stop a lender from pulling money out of their account with remotely created checks the borrower never signed; and their sensitive financial information could not be sold by lead-generation websites to a stream of lenders. Prepaid debit users would no longer be charged overdraft fees, and tribal members would benefit from a study of lending conditions on reservations.

how_it_helps.text: Small-dollar lenders (loans up to $5,000, repaid within a year) must register with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau before issuing credit [S2].

Online or telephone small-dollar loans must comply with the annual percentage rate, interest, and fee laws of the state where the borrower lives, closing the 'rent-a-bank' and internet-lender route around state rate caps [S2].

Remotely created checks — payment orders the consumer never signed — could only be issued against a consumer's account if the consumer named that person in writing at their bank, and the consumer could revoke that permission at any time [S2].
Lenders could not issue a payment order as retaliation when a consumer exercises any right under federal consumer financial law [S2].
One-time electronic fund transfers used to repay small-dollar credit get the same protections the law gives preauthorized transfers, and fees for overdrafting a prepaid account are banned [S2].

Lead generators — websites that collect a borrower's Social Security number and bank details and sell them to lenders — may not operate in small-dollar lending unless they are the direct lender, and must identify themselves for service of process [S2].

The Government Accountability Office must study capital availability and the impact of small-dollar credit on tribal members, in consultation with the CFPB, Federal Reserve, Bureau of Indian Affairs, tribes, and community development lenders [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Small-dollar lenders, lead-generation platforms, and banks that profit from overdraft and account-access fees. Lenders that rely on charging triple-digit annual rates online would lose the ability to export a more permissive state's law to borrowers everywhere. Lead-generation sites would lose their core business of auctioning borrowers' financial data. Banks would lose overdraft fee income on prepaid accounts and would have to honor consumers' controls over unsigned payment orders.

drawbacks.text: The bill relies on CFPB rulemaking to define and extend coverage, so its reach would depend on future administrations: the Bureau can raise the $5,000 cap, lengthen repayment terms, and expand the definition of covered transactions, and a different administration could write narrower rules [S2].

A good-faith objection: capping fees and restricting collection tools without expanding access to affordable small-dollar credit can push marginal borrowers toward worse alternatives — unregulated lenders, utility shutoffs, or going without — which is the standard industry and some economists' argument against payday restrictions; the bill's tribal-lending study acknowledges that credit access on reservations is already a problem [S2].

The lead-generation ban exempts ordinary internet infrastructure — telecommunications services, internet access, hosting, and content transmission — so sophisticated data brokers could potentially restructure their operations to fit the exemption [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The borrower protections are concrete and address well-documented harms: unsignable 'remotely created checks' have been a workhorse of online payday lending, lead generators routinely pass consumers' Social Security numbers and account details to multiple lenders in seconds, and prepaid overdraft fees fall on the lowest-balance users. The main honest cost is on the other side of the ledger — restricting the supply of high-cost credit helps people who escape the loans but can hurt people who relied on them and have no better option, and the bill pairs restrictions with no new source of affordable small-dollar credit. The design is sound as consumer protection, but incomplete on the access side.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late September 2024 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, and the Congress ended in January 2025 with no hearing, no vote, and no action since referral.

narrative.text: Representative Suzanne Bonamici of Oregon introduced the bill on September 19, 2024, joined by Representatives Jayapal, Garcia of Texas, and Porter as original cosponsors [S2].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day, which was the only congressional action it ever received [S4].
The bill ended the 118th Congress in committee with four additional cosponsors, all Democrats, and no reported floor or committee action [S3], [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Small-dollar online lenders, lead-generation platforms, and banks collecting overdraft and account-access fees are better off, because the restrictions would never take effect. Borrowers remain exposed to the practices the bill targeted. Representative Bonamici and the cosponsors can reintroduce it, but its committee inaction means the determining factor was simply the committee's decision never to schedule it.

sides.party_line_note: All five supporters — the sponsor and four cosponsors — were Democrats, and no Republican cosponsor ever joined; the bill never advanced far enough to produce a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill requires registration with the CFPB and forces online and bank-conduit loans to obey the borrower's own state's rate and fee caps, which would erase the core profit mechanism of lenders charging triple-digit annual rates across state lines. Borrowers' cost of credit is exactly the lenders' revenue, so the industry's interest runs against the public's here.

industries.industry: Lead-generation platforms selling borrowers' financial data
industries.note: The bill bans anyone who is not the direct lender from collecting and distributing small-dollar applicants' Social Security numbers and bank details, eliminating the pay-per-lead business model. Consumers currently lose control of their most sensitive financial information the moment they fill out one of these forms.

Banks would lose overdraft fee income on prepaid accounts and must honor consumers' written designations revoking access for remotely created checks. Prepaid overdraft fees fall disproportionately on low-balance users.

industries.industry: Online payment processors and internet intermediaries
industries.note: The bill creates new limits on unsigned remotely created checks that flow through the payment system, a compliance cost, but expressly exempts telecommunications providers, internet access services, and pure hosting or transmission functions from the lead-generation restrictions.
